title: Choosing an ideal client and a training specialty
audience: Owners and lead trainers or therapists setting up or refining who their service is for
learningOutcomes: Write a one-sentence ideal-client statement from a set of real client records
Explain why a specialty narrows the market and still leaves room for referrals to other providers
Check a specialty and its refusal criteria against the scope and the anti-discrimination rules.

instruction.heading: A specialty states who you serve and the result you deliver
instruction.body: A specialty is a short, plain answer to two questions: who you work with, and what change they can expect. It need not be a clever slogan. Its job is to let a prospect see quickly that the service is meant for them. Many providers avoid narrowing because they fear losing work. In practice a clear focus makes marketing easier to write, makes referrals easier for other people to pass on, and lets you build repeatable skills for one kind of client.

instruction.heading: Build the profile from records, not guesses
instruction.body: Start with the clients who have stayed longest and reached what they came for. Look for patterns in goals, weekly availability, distance from the business, how they found you, and what they say they value. Record the patterns in a short table. A profile built from memory tends to describe the clients you wish you had. A profile built from records shows the clients you already serve well.

instruction.heading: Say who you refer on, and why
instruction.body: Every specialty leaves some enquiries outside its scope. Explain the fit and refer the person to a suitable provider, rather than deflecting without a reason. Declining someone because of age, disability, sex, race or another protected attribute can breach anti-discrimination law. Health suitability is screened through its own process, not through the specialty.

procedure: Pull the records of your ten longest-standing clients and note each one's main goal, weekly availability and enquiry source.
Keep only the traits that appear in at least half of those records.
Write one sentence: who you help, the change they seek, and how you deliver it.
List the enquiries you would refer on, and the type of provider you would refer them to.
Check each refusal criterion against the anti-discrimination rules, and leave out any legal point that is not checked.

workedExamples.situation: A hypothetical mobile massage therapist finds that seven of ten long-term clients are office workers who book after work and want help with neck and shoulder tension between visits.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Which ideal-client sentence do the records support?
workedExamples.reasoning: The sentence should name the working pattern and the common concern, because both come from the records. A sentence about anyone who wants to relax is too broad to guide marketing. A sentence about age or income is not supported by the records and could create a refusal problem.

equipmentAndPpe: Client booking history, with only the fields the profile needs

commonErrors.error: A specialty so broad it fits every enquiry
commonErrors.prevention: Test the sentence: if a stranger cannot tell from it whether they are the right client, narrow it.

commonErrors.error: Using screening questions to judge a person's worth or ability to pay
commonErrors.prevention: Screen only for fit with the service, and for health suitability through the proper process.
Build the statement from your own client records.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Refusing or steering prospects by a protected attribute may breach anti-discrimination law. Check Australian rules and exceptions with a qualified adviser before writing refusal criteria.
This lesson does not grant any registration, licence or qualification, and does not confirm that a specialty is permitted by any regulator.

qualityStandard: The ideal-client sentence traces to at least five client records
Each referral or refusal criterion is tied to the service, and unchecked legal points are left out
documentationEvidence: Profile table with record counts (no names)
Signed ideal-client sentence with the date written
summary: A specialty says who you serve and what change they can expect.
Build it from records of your best-fit clients.
Refer on with a reason; check the law before any refusal criterion.

knowledgeChecks.question: What does a useful specialty state?
options: A full list of every service you could offer
Who you serve and the change they can expect from you
The lowest price in your area with no other detail

knowledgeChecks.question: A prospect is outside your specialty. Which first step fits best?
options: Explain the fit and refer them to a suitable provider
Quote a price for the work and take the booking anyway
Ask their age and decline if it is above a set number

knowledgeChecks.question: Which information best supports a client profile?
options: A guess about what people in the area can afford and what the nearby gyms charge
Patterns from long-term clients, such as goals, schedule and how they found you
Competitors' prices and their advertising copy, collected each week
